1:
Manasseh's lot needs explaining before it can be described, because this tribe receives twice. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, say the historian pauses here precisely to note that the Manassites held a double inheritance, and that the clause "for he was the firstborn of Joseph" is the reason given for it: on that account, over and above the territory already his in Gilead and Bashan, he received a second allotment inside Canaan proper. They also unpick the grammar, showing that "to Machir" stands absolutely at the head of the sentence and is then resumed — to Machir were Gilead and Bashan assigned, because he was a man of war, having earned a claim to those lands by the bravery he showed in conquering them.

The title "firstborn" is the difficulty, since Jacob had crossed his hands and preferred Ephraim. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, resolves it by distinguishing prominence from privilege: Ephraim was to be the more numerous and powerful, but Manasseh was the firstborn and kept the firstborn's right, the double portion, which is why this half tribe is not folded into Ephraim but has a lot of its own like its brethren beyond Jordan. Adam Clarke says the same in fewer words — Jacob's blessing at Genesis 48:19-20 set Ephraim before Manasseh in a certain sense, but this passage shows the preference did not touch the rights of primogeniture. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, reports Bishop Patrick's proposal to translate the clause concessively — though he was the firstborn of Joseph — which yields the same sense from the other side: the second lot fell to Manasseh because, firstborn or not, Jacob had preferred his brother.

About Machir himself the witnesses differ over whether a man or a family is meant. Clarke thinks it cannot be Machir in person, who would by now be nearly two hundred years old, and reads the verse of his children, who possessed the lot originally designed for their father; his descendants, being of a warlike and intrepid spirit, were well qualified to defend an exposed frontier. Wesley calls Machir the only son of Manasseh and so takes the name to stand for the whole tribe, adding that his posterity were no degenerate sons but had his valiant blood still in their veins. Henry supplies a possible occasion for the reputation — Machir was born in Egypt, and may have distinguished himself in the quarrel between the Ephraimites and the men of Gath (1 Chronicles 7:21) — while conceding that the particular history is not recorded. Wesley notes that "Gilead and Bashan" must mean part of those countries, since portions of them went to Reuben and Gad.

The rest of Manasseh, the half that had no share beyond Jordan, is then set down by families: Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida, the male children of Manasseh. The reformed John Gill and Keil and Delitzsch both take these as the six houses among which the western lot would be divided; Henry matches them against the census list at Numbers 26:30-32, where the same six appear with Abiezer under the form Jezeer. Clarke, holding that Manasseh had no son but Machir, reads "the rest of the children" as grandchildren, very probably the children of Gilead the son of Machir. Wesley notes why the text says male children at all: the word is there to prepare for what comes next.
3:
What comes next is a family with no sons in it. Zelophehad, of the house of Hepher, left five daughters — Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah — and the reformed John Gill notes that his descent is traced in full, through Hepher and Gilead and Machir to Manasseh, precisely to establish the claim his daughters are about to make. Adam Clarke refers the case back to Numbers 27:1-7 and Numbers 36:1. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, summarise the history: these women had petitioned Moses for a separate portion in the promised land and their request had been granted, so they now come before the committee appointed to divide it and repeat the promise, which is at once fulfilled.

John Calvin, reformed, is interested in why they had to come at all. The decision was already given from the mouth of the Lord, and no one had dared say a word against it; yet had they kept silent, he thinks no regard would have been paid to them. Men are so tenacious of their own interests that it seldom occurs to them to give others their due — so the daughters apply to Joshua and Eleazar and insist on not being deprived of a legitimate succession. Calvin is careful to add that nobody obstructed them: Joshua interposed no delay and the people did not murmur. His conclusion is measured: all were disposed to act equitably; every one was simply occupied with his own concerns and too apt to overlook another's. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, draws the same lesson forward — these women had pleaded their own cause before Moses when they were young, and now would not lose the benefit of that grant for want of speaking to Joshua. Nor did Joshua object that women who had not served in the wars of Canaan had no business in its possessions; he readily gave them an inheritance among their father's brethren. Henry turns it into a warning: those who take care in this world's wilderness to make sure of a place among the saints in light will have the comfort of it hereafter, and those who neglect it now will lose it for ever.

The arithmetic that follows has puzzled every commentator here. Ten portions fell to Manasseh besides Gilead and Bashan, and with six sons and five daughters in view the number will not obviously come out. Wesley's solution is the simplest: five portions for the surviving sons and five for the daughters, Hepher and Zelophehad both being dead without male issue and so drawing nothing themselves. Clarke arrives at the same result by the same subtraction, following Calmet, and pauses over the word rendered "portions," which literally means cords or cables — a hint, he thinks, that the land was measured with a line, and evidence of more geographical skill than is usually granted them. Gill reports the Talmudic reckoning preserved by Jarchi and Kimchi, that the six families took six parts and the daughters four, on account of their father, of their grandfather Hepher as firstborn, and of a childless uncle; but he prefers the plainer account, that Hepher's single portion was divided into five among Zelophehad's daughters.

Calvin will not accept any of these. He says bluntly that some expositors disguise the difficulty and others, unable to solve it, trifle; that four portions for five daughters is absurd; and that doubling their share because their father was firstborn is no better. His own view is that the exact number of families among whom the division ran cannot now be recovered, so the sum cannot be checked — and that the honest thing is to say so, holding only that mutual equity was observed. Wesley adds the point the whole passage exists to make: the daughters received not less than the sons, the sex being no bar to their inheritance.
7:
Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, gives the shape of the territory before the details crowd in: it ran from Jordan on the east to the great sea on the west, lay all along contiguous to Ephraim on the south, and abutted on Asher and Issachar to the north — Asher north-west, Issachar north-east. That is how he reads the closing clause of the description, that Manasseh and Ephraim, both together making the tribe of Joseph, met in Asher on the north and in Issachar on the east, since Ephraim by itself reached neither.

The line begins at Asher, and the reformed John Gill immediately warns against the obvious reading. This is not the border of the tribe of Asher, which lay far too distant, but a town of that name inside Manasseh; in Jerome's day a village so called was still shown fifteen miles from Neapolis on the road to Scythopolis, near the public way. From there the boundary passes Michmethah before Shechem and runs to the inhabitants of En-tappuah, and here the arrangement becomes intricate in a way the witnesses think significant. Manasseh had the land of Tappuah, all the fields and villages of that territory; the town of Tappuah itself, sitting on Manasseh's border, belonged to Ephraim. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, note that this southern boundary coincides with the northern boundary of Ephraim already described, and is given here only with greater precision at certain points.

The line then descends to the river Kanah. Gill observes that the same watercourse marked Ephraim's border, Ephraim lying north of it there and Manasseh south of it here. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, translates the name literally as the river or valley of the reeds, the vallis arundineti of the Vulgate, and takes it for Manasseh's northern limit with the Mediterranean as its southern one. Wesley identifies the cities of Ephraim that lie among the cities of Manasseh as Tappuah and those on the coast descending to the river, and thinks the intermixture neither strange nor unfitting between two tribes linked by so near an alliance.

How the two tribes "met together in Asher on the north, and in Issachar on the east" is the knot of the passage, and Clarke works at it geographically. Asher extended from the Mediterranean to Mount Carmel, and Manasseh reached to Dor and her towns in the neighbourhood of Carmel, so the two formed a junction at the sea. He allows that the tribes were genuinely intermingled in several cases — Manasseh had towns in both Issachar and Asher, Judah had towns in Dan and Simeon, Simeon had towns in Judah — and suggests that what is said of boundaries may sometimes mean the towns one tribe held inside another's limits, some of them apparently exchanged or purchased by mutual consent, so that possessions overlapped without the tribes themselves being confused. Wesley reaches the same place by a different route: Zebulun came between Asher and the house of Joseph for most of the distance, but some necks of land belonging to Ephraim and Manasseh jutted out further than the rest and touched Asher's border.

Henry draws the conclusion the geography keeps pressing. There was great communication between this tribe and Ephraim — Tappuah's town in one and its country in the other, cities of Ephraim standing inside Manasseh's border — and God so ordered it that although no tribe's inheritance might be alienated, the tribes should nonetheless interlock, keeping up acquaintance and correspondence and giving occasion for good offices one to another, as became men who though of different tribes were all one Israel.
11:
Beyond its borders Manasseh held six towns with their dependent villages inside the territory of Issachar and Asher: Beth-shean, Ibleam, Dor, En-dor, Taanach and Megiddo. The reformed John Gill notes the symmetry — as Ephraim had cities inside Manasseh, so Manasseh had cities inside these two tribes that bordered it — and that Beth-shean, lying in Issachar, was the furthest reach of Manasseh in that direction.

Beth-shean draws most of the comment because it had the longest afterlife. Gill reports from Josephus that it was later called Scythopolis, and rejects Pliny's derivation of the name from the Scythians, preferring to trace it to Succoth, where Jacob had lived not far off. He places it at the entrance of the great plain of Jezreel, six hundred furlongs — some seventy-five miles — from Jerusalem on the reckoning of the books of Maccabees, counts it among the cities of the Decapolis from which our Lord had hearers, and passes on the Talmudic compliment that if the garden of Eden were in the land of Israel, Beth-shean was the gate of it. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, gives the same later name with a different explanation, deriving Scythopolis from the Cuthites planted in the Samaritan cities by the kings of Assyria. He places Dor on the Mediterranean about eight miles from Caesarea on the road to Tyre, and identifies En-dor, the well or fountain of Dor, as the place where Saul went to consult the woman with a familiar spirit (1 Samuel 28:7).

John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, explains how a tribe comes to hold towns outside its own lot: when one portion proved too narrow and the next too large, part was moved across, as Simeon's whole inheritance was taken inside Judah's when Judah's proved too big. He observes that what Manasseh received here included the inhabitants and not merely the places, the people being spared and used as servants; and he offers an alternative rendering of the closing phrase, that instead of "three countries" it may mean the third part of that country — a third of the portion of Issachar and Asher in which these towns lay.

John Calvin, reformed, finds the arrangement hard to account for and says so. How Manasseh came to hold cities in the lots of Asher and Issachar, with Ephraim's territory lying between, is not easy to divine; perhaps a more commodious dwelling was thought less likely to breed complaints, or perhaps, once the country was better known, some adjustment was made on grounds of equity to the earlier partition. His own preference is to read this as a later acquisition, made when it was discovered that Manasseh could occupy a wider extent without loss to anyone. He raises a second difficulty too: how could cities be granted in Asher and Issachar when the portions of those tribes were not yet settled? His answer is that the narrative here anticipates, relating what had not yet taken place. And he insists the grant was not of a subdued country ready to be enjoyed, but an inheritance held in hope, founded more on heavenly promise than on possession.
12:
The promise held in hope was not made good. Manasseh could not drive out the inhabitants of those six cities; the Canaanites would dwell in that land; and when Israel afterwards grew strong they put them to tribute instead of dispossessing them. The reformed John Gill offers two readings of the failure and does not force a choice: either they had not the strength at first, or they were negligent and slothful, let the Canaanites remain, and lost the advantage, so that by the time they might have acted their neighbours had grown too numerous for them.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, presses the harder of those readings. They had neither grace nor courage to go against their enemies, and preferred sharing their territory with a people the justice of God had proscribed to the exertion of expelling them. He then offers a second construction of the Hebrew that other commentators prefer, and reports it fairly: not that Manasseh could not drive them out, but that the children of Manasseh could not resolve to destroy those cities, and the Canaanites consented to dwell in the land — an arrangement both sides found tolerable, the one paying tribute and the other choosing to tolerate them on those terms. On either reading, Clarke thinks the tribute came later, when the children of Israel had waxen strong, which is what the text itself goes on to say. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, state the sequence without comment: the Manassites were unable to exterminate the Canaanites from these six towns and the districts round them, but when they grew stronger they made them tributary and still did not utterly drive them out. Gill notes that by then it was not Manasseh alone that had grown strong but the other tribes with them.

John Calvin, reformed, will allow neither the excuse of weakness nor the excuse of prudence. The lot that assigned those cities was an indubitable pledge of victory, so the reason they could not expel the inhabitants was that they were not fully persuaded God is true, and stifled his working by their own sluggishness. That is the first fault. The second he thinks less pardonable still: having it in their power to destroy all, they were not merely slow to execute the command but, drawn by filthy lucre, preserved alive the very people God had doomed. Calvin puts his finger on what tribute actually means — those on whom we impose it we take, in a manner, under our faith and protection. God had appointed Israel the ministers of his vengeance and supplied them with strength for it; they delayed, and in delaying deprived themselves of the liberty of acting rightly. He does not find it strange that God punished this perverse heartlessness by making the spared nations thorns in their eyes and pricks in their sides. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, adds only that they served their own ends by conniving at them, and that the Manassites may have learned the practice from Ephraim, and excused themselves by that example.
14:
The complaint is the first note of discontent in the division of the land, and every witness here treats it as ill-founded. The children of Joseph ask why they have been given but one lot and one portion, seeing they are a great people whom the LORD has blessed. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, say flatly that there was no real ground for it, and reach for the census: at the second numbering in Moses' time Ephraim stood at thirty-two thousand five hundred and Manasseh at fifty-two thousand seven hundred, so that Ephraim and half Manasseh together did not amount to what the grievance implies. They also gloss the two phrases carefully — "so far" of degree, "hitherto" of time — and note that the "me" of the complaint is the house of Joseph speaking as one.

The reformed John Gill asks who exactly is speaking. Some understand it of the Manassites only, and he grants that the complaint and its arguments fit them best; but the Ephraimites were certainly present at the interview, and if they did not join in the request expressly, they countenanced and encouraged it by being there. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, supplies the occasion — they had gone and seen the portion allotted them and found it far short of expectation — and offers two senses for "one portion": either they really had but one lot, afterwards divided between them by arbitrators, or the land severally allotted was scarcely enough for one of the two.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, suspects a motive behind the timing. Joshua was himself of Ephraim, and they probably promised themselves some particular favour, expecting not to be held so strictly to the decision of the lot as the other tribes had been. Joshua's refusal is the point Henry wants: in the discharge of a public office he had no more regard to his own tribe than to any other, and administered impartially, without favour or affection — an example, Henry says, to all in public trusts. He notices too how the words are chosen. What was in fact a competent provision they call in disdain "but one lot," as though what was assigned to both were scarcely enough for one; and he glosses the complainers of Jude 16 as men who blame their lot. Yet Henry will not let their own better instinct pass unremarked: they speak thankfully of the increase God has given them without presuming on its continuance — the Lord has blessed me hitherto — and the uncertainty of what may come should never make us unthankful for what has been.

John Calvin, reformed, weighs whether the complaint was even factually true and decides it was, though dishonestly used. He cannot believe the dividers blundered so grossly as to throw two tribes into one lot, since Ephraim and Manasseh were plainly two stems and the land was reckoned in ten; and Joshua's answer, which never denies the charge, tells against a flat denial being available. His resolution is that one lot did serve for both by design, because the two were brothers of one father and it was expedient that their settlements should adjoin — and that no injustice followed, since a lot fixed locality without fixing limits, which were enlarged or curtailed according to numbers. The falsehood, Calvin says, lay elsewhere: in counting as nothing everything that still had to be won by warlike prowess, as though the lot had assigned the other tribes only subjugated ground.
15:
Joshua's reply takes their own premise and hands it back. If thou be a great people, then get thee up to the wood country, and cut down for thyself there in the land of the Perizzites and of the giants, if mount Ephraim be too narrow for thee. The reformed John Gill says in a phrase what the whole answer does — he retorts their own argument upon them — and John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, spells it out: seeing thou art a great and numerous people, turn thy complaints into action and enlarge thy borders by thy own hand, where thou mayest confidently expect God's assistance.

Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, is careful about what Joshua does and does not concede. He would not reverse the decision of the lot; not a boundary is moved. What he grants is permission — since there was much woodland, they might clear away as much of it as they needed and extend themselves as far as they pleased. The grievance is answered with a licence to work rather than with a redrawing of the map.

Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, take the sending-away as the substance of the reply and explain what clearing the wood would mean: making room for houses, fields and meadows by felling the trees. They also locate the ground. "Mount Ephraim" is used here proleptically, of the range that took its name from the tribe just settled on it — a limestone chain running from Kirjath-jearim, where the mountains of Judah end, to the plain of Jezreel, and taking in most of Benjamin's territory as well; and the wood Joshua speaks of is distinguished in the text from that range.

Wesley identifies the inhabitants Joshua names. The Perizzites he supposes a savage and brutish sort who lived in woods and mountains, and the giants a people of the caves and hills, driven there now that they had lost their cities. He also reads the last clause concessively rather than conditionally — seeing mount Ephraim is too narrow for thee, as thou complainest, take to thyself the rest of that hilly and wooded country — and observes that mount Ephraim, strictly the portion of one tribe, stands here for the whole allotment of Ephraim and Manasseh together, since the complaint had been that their whole portion was too strait, not merely one part of it.

Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, presses the answer into a proverb. Joshua bids them work for more: let all hands cut down the trees, rid the rough land, and make it by art and industry good arable ground. Many wish for larger possessions who never cultivate what they have, and think they deserve more talents while trading with none. Most people's poverty, Henry says, is the effect of their idleness; would they dig, they need not beg.
16:
The reply does not satisfy them, and their counter-argument closes both roads at once. The hill is not enough for us; and as for the plain, all the Canaanites who dwell in the valley have chariots of iron, both those of Beth-shean and her towns and those of the valley of Jezreel. The reformed John Gill gives two possible senses of the first clause. Either they mean the wooded highland will not suffice even if they win it and clear it, or — reading the Hebrew as "cannot be found by us" — they mean they are unable to get it into their hands at all, there being a valley of enemies between them and it. John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, takes the second sense: the hill will not be obtained by us, since the Perizzites and the giants have the advantage of the woods and mountains and will easily frustrate the attempt. He then reads the rest as their anticipation of the obvious rejoinder — if you say we may go down and take more land in the pleasant and fruitful valleys, we shall meet no less difficulty there.

On the chariots the witnesses agree about the fact and about the fear. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, explains them as very strong chariots armed with scythes, as is generally supposed, and takes the hill of the complaint to be Gilboa, which had fallen to them by lot. Wesley describes them as not made of iron but armed with it, for offence as well as defence, having scythes and swords fastened to them to cut down whatever stood in the way. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, says they mowed men down like corn, and states the complaint in its strongest form: they had a good portion, but it was in bad hands, and they could not come at it — they would rather have been given a country already reduced.

Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, take the geography seriously enough to map it. The land of the valley covers both the Jordan valley near Beisan and the plain of Jezreel that opens into it nearby; that plain, named from the town, is the great field called Esdrelom in Judith and the great plain in Josephus, and is the Merj Ibn Aamer of their own day, running south-west from the Mediterranean above Carmel and reaching almost to the Jordan. It is, in other words, exactly the country where chariots are worth having.

John Calvin, reformed, treats the whole speech as evasion. They quibble as much as they can to avoid following a suggestion than which nothing was more reasonable: the mountain is called rugged and half a desert, so that adding it would profit them little, while the cultivated plain is said to be barred to them by the enemy's array. Their appeal to the iron chariots he finds the worst of it — as though they had not already learned by experience that the Lord could trample down horses and chariots without difficulty.
17:
Joshua does not change his answer; he repeats it with the reasons attached. Keil and Delitzsch, grammatical-historical, read that as deliberate — the reply of the children of Joseph had shown cowardice and want of confidence in God's help, so Joshua contented himself with saying the same thing again, more fully. Thou art a great people and hast great power; there shall not be one lot only to thee. Because thou art numerous and strong, they gloss, one lot shall not remain thy limit: thou canst and wilt extend thine inheritance. The mountain shall be thine, for it is wood and thou shalt cut it down, and its outgoings shall be thine — by which they understand not the highland already allotted to Ephraim but the wooded hills Joshua had pointed to, and by the outgoings the fields and plains bordering the forest.

The reformed John Gill notes that Joshua addressed the house of Joseph, naming Ephraim and Manasseh both, which settles that men of each were present; and since the two were brethren with united interests and intermixed cities, an enlargement would serve them jointly — Manasseh needing it the more, having more of its allotted cities still in Canaanite hands than any other tribe. On the promise itself Gill is content to say what it costs to believe: the mountain shall be thine, thou shalt get possession of it, though the difficulties in the way seem insuperable.

John Wesley, wesleyan-arminian, unfolds "not one lot only" as a promise conditional on effort — thou needest and deservest more than the lot thou art actually possessed of, and thou hast power to get more; endeavour it, and God will bless thee and give thee more. He identifies the outgoings as the valleys and fields adjoining the highland, which is precisely where the Canaanites and their chariots were. Adam Clarke, wesleyan-arminian, turns that into strategy: clear the wood, occupy the mountain, and you will soon command the valleys; holding the defiles of the country you will drive out the Canaanites, iron chariots and all, your position being advantageous, your numbers respectable, and the hand of God upon you for good.

Clarke closes the chapter with three reflections. Israel was hard to please and rarely content, and the children of Joseph were inclined to quarrel with Joshua over a lot they could not have been ignorant was determined by God's own providence. Joshua was firm: he would not alter the appointment of God and saw no reason to change the grant, since a numerous and strong people exerting itself under ordinary providence had every reason to expect success. And slothfulness is natural to man — many profess to trust God's mercy while never labouring to enter into his rest, and God will not reverse his purpose to accommodate their idleness. Matthew Henry, puritan-evangelical, makes the same point about ourselves rather than about them: we straiten ourselves by imagining the difficulties in the way of our enlargement to be greater than they really are, when nothing is insuperable to faith and holy resolution.
